families.s: HSE design codes for buildings and structures at major-hazard plant
families.t: foreseeable loads, structural integrity, containment, occupied buildings, supports, fire, explosion and lifecycle
f: Buildings and structures may protect plant, house control systems or provide accommodation and shelter.
They can form part of the strategy to prevent, control or mitigate major accidents.
Structural failure near major-hazard plant can initiate or escalate a hazardous event.
Buildings and structures should withstand foreseeable loadings and operational extremes through their design life.
Design should consider fire, explosion, impact and environmental loading where relevant.
Supports for process plant should maintain integrity under credible accident conditions.
Occupied buildings require particular consideration of location and resistance to major-hazard effects.
Inspection and maintenance should preserve the safety functions assumed in the design.
families.g: Foreseeable loads, structural integrity, containment, occupied buildings, supports, fire, explosion and lifecycle guidance is general process-safety evidence and does not prove current controls, condition, inventory, performance or exact risk at an individual parcel.

families.s: HSE jetty design, operation and maintenance for hazardous-substance transfer
families.t: ship-shore transfer, fire, explosion, toxic release, corrosion, marine pollution, mooring, pipework and emergency isolation
f: Major-hazard jetties are used to load or unload hazardous substances between ships and land storage.
Jetty incidents can develop into major accidents.
Credible outcomes include fire, explosion, toxic release, corrosive release and marine pollution.
Design should prevent and effectively contain foreseeable releases of dangerous substances.
Operation and maintenance should reflect marine loading, impact, corrosion and environmental exposure.
Transfer pipework, hoses, arms and connections require suitable design and inspection.
Mooring and ship movement should be controlled so transfer equipment is not overstressed.
Emergency shutdown, isolation, communication and access arrangements should be coordinated between ship and shore.
families.g: Ship-shore transfer, fire, explosion, toxic release, corrosion, marine pollution, mooring, pipework and emergency isolation guidance is general process-safety evidence and does not prove current controls, condition, inventory, performance or exact risk at an individual parcel.

families.t: standards, components, pressure, temperature, supports, flexibles, joints, valves, inspection and competence
f: Process pipework is a primary means of conveying fluids in process industries.
Pipework integrity depends on design, construction and maintenance throughout plant life.
Pipework systems include pipes, flanges, supports, gaskets, bolts, valves, strainers, flexibles and expansion joints.
Design should use nationally accepted standards and competent mechanical and process designers.
Materials and ratings should match pressure, temperature, chemical service and foreseeable loads.
Supports and flexibility should control weight, thermal movement, vibration and external loading.
Joints, valves and flexible connections should be selected and maintained to minimise loss of containment.
Inspection and management of modifications should preserve the original design basis.

families.s: HSE process-plant design codes and inherently safer design
families.t: design codes, pressure, temperature, materials, vessels, reactors, heat exchangers, boilers, rotating equipment and commissioning
f: Process-plant design should apply relevant codes, standards and competent multidisciplinary engineering.
Inherently safer design should be considered before reliance on protective systems.
Temperature, pressure, materials and corrosion are core design considerations.
Mechanical design should address pressure vessels, storage tanks, reactors and heat exchangers.
Furnaces, boilers and rotating equipment require equipment-specific safety considerations.
Structural design should include foreseeable environmental and lightning loads where relevant.
Special storage cases include chlorine, ammonia, LPG and hydrocarbons.
Construction and commissioning should verify that plant matches the design and is fit for service.

families.s: HSE drum and cylinder storage and handling
families.t: toxic substances, flammable substances, inventories, siting, movement, connection, separation, leak control and emergency response
f: Drums and cylinders are commonly used to store and transport toxic and flammable chemicals.
A single compressed or liquefied toxic-gas cylinder can present a significant hazard.
Large stores can create substantial total inventories despite small individual containers.
Movement and connection or disconnection bring operators close to the hazard and create potential for human error.
Storage location should consider material hazards, inventory and separation from plant, traffic and occupied buildings.
Containers should be protected against impact, damage, heat and uncontrolled movement.
Incompatible materials should be segregated and leaks should be detected and contained.
Operating, maintenance, training and emergency procedures should cover the actual drum and cylinder tasks.
families.g: Toxic substances, flammable substances, inventories, siting, movement, connection, separation, leak control and emergency response guidance is general process-safety evidence and does not prove current controls, condition, inventory, performance or exact risk at an individual parcel.
